newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOTOR RACING-RELAXED HILL DISMISSES FAVOURITISM CLAIMS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-RELAXED HILL DISMISSES FAVOURITISM CLAIMS.

text.p: A relaxed Damon Hill on Thursday dismissed claims that his Williams team would show favouritism to team mate and arch-rival Jacques Villeneuve in Sunday's deciding Japanese Grand Prix.

The 35-year-old Englishman, who needs only one point from the race to clinch his first world drivers' title, said there was no chance the Williams team, powered by Renault engines, would give preference to either driver.
"Any thoughts that there may be a preference are wrong," he stated firmly, as he gave an impromptu news conference in the Williams team garage surrounded by dozens of reporters.
"Frank (Williams) and Patrick (Head) want to see fair play and both drivers have got a fair and equal chance."

Hill's comments came only four days after fellow Briton Jackie Stewart, the three-times world champion who is launching his own new grand prix team next season, had hinted at the possibility of technical interference favouring Villeneuve.

In a report in the Independent on Sunday newspaper in London, Stewart said: "There is also the sneaking concern that the suppliers, the sponsors and the team itself must all stand to profit considerably more from Jacques Villeneuve being world champion than Damon Hill because they would lose Damon immediately.
"We are not talking simply about morals, and we should all have them at the highest level, but we are talking about enormous commercial interests and loyalties."

Stewart's comments sparked a succession of countering remarks including those of Renault Sport president Patrick Faure who said: "I have never attached the slightest importance to having the number one. What counts in Formula One is being the first across the line on a Sunday, whatever the number of the car."
Hill, fresh from five days rest and acclimatisation in Hong Kong, was in a relaxed frame of mind as he met the media on the eve of his final grand prix with Williams.
He said he faced a dilemma about his strategy, but would attack hard in qualifying in order to try and gain pole position and then deal with his strategic thinking after that.

"I could try to win and take risks or I could drive for the championship," he said. "Winning the championship is more important and that is what I have to weigh up in my mind...How to do it. Take a risk or just go for points."
He said he also felt nervous about being overly cautious and pointed out that all the pressure would be on Villeneuve, who needs to win to keep his title hopes alive.

"Jacques has more pressure on him because he has to win if he is to win the championship, but he can just do what he wants. For me, it is crucial to come away from this race saying I am the world champion. That is the most important thing of all."
Even if Villeneuve wins the race, Hill only needs to cross the line sixth to capture the drivers' title after finishing runner-up for the past two seasons.

Villeneuve admitted his own hopes of victory and the championship were "slim", but added: "I really have nothing to lose. I'll go out and give it my best shot to try and win the race and then we will see what happens."
He added that he felt no emotions about the tussle with Hill, despite the fact that their relationship as team mates had put them under strain in the title race.
"There is not hate, nothing like that," he said, adding that these kind of emotions contribute to drivers' making mistakes because they cloud their judgement.
